# Abstract

The archaeological landscape of extra-Amazonian Southern and South-Eastern Brazil encompasses 1.920.483 km² between latitudes 14°S and 34°S, spanning Atlantic coastal lagoons, the Serra do Mar escarpments, the Araucária highlands of the southern plateau, the semi-deciduous forests of the Upper Paraná basin, and the seasonal inundation plains of the Pantanal and Rio Grande do Sul. Across this diverse macro-region, human settlement evolved across eleven millennia from sparse terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene foraging bands into monumental littoral shell-mound communities, nucleated highland semi-subterranean villages and expansive agro-fluvial networks. At European contact in 1500AD, the aggregate indigenous population of Southern Brazil reached approximately 1.200.000 persons (with a credible interval of 984.000 to 1.416.000), representing an overall regional density of 0,62 persons/km².

Long-run demographic expansion in Southern Brazil was characterised by marked geographical asymmetry and distinct ecological thresholds. Along the Atlantic shoreline, monumental shell mounds or sambaquis proliferated between 5000BC and 1000BC, sustained by exceptionally productive estuarine and marine fisheries that supported sedentary populations with local densities exceeding 3 persons/km² along linear coastal strips. In the southern highlands, the cooling late Holocene climate favoured the expansion of Brazilian pine forests (*Araucária angustifolia*), providing an abundant carbohydrate anchor that fuelled the demic surge of Southern Proto-Jê groups (Taquara-Itararé tradition) from 800AD onward, evidenced by dense concentrations of pit-houses, mound enclosures and funerary earthworks. Concurrently, the subtropical floodplains of the Paraná, Paranapanema and Uruguay rivers became conduits for the rapid territorial advance of Guarani horticulturalists, whose slash-and-burn polyculture supported nucleated villages numbering several hundred to upwards of 3.000 inhabitants.

This study reconstructs the long-run demographic trajectory of Southern and South-Eastern Brazil across six hydrological sub-regions: the Southeast Atlantic Coast, the Southern Atlantic Sambaqui and Lagoa dos Patos Belt, the Upper Paraná and Central Cerrado, the Tietê, Paranapanema and Iguaçu basins, the Pantanal and Upper Paraguay Basin, and the Uruguay Basin with the Rio Grande do Sul Pampa. Drawing upon a geo-referenced gazetteer of 1.482 systematically catalogued archaeological sites and primary ethnohistorical records, we trace regional growth from an initial baseline of 15.040 persons in 10000BC to 158.000 in 5000BC, 553.600 at the turn of the Common Era in 0AD, and 1.200.000 in 1500AD. By grounding quantitative estimates in carrying capacity models, site densities and radiocarbon chronologies, this work provides an empirical foundation for comparative Pre-Columbian demography in eastern South America.

# Regional Geography and Environmental Endowment

## Macro-Geomorphological Setting and River Basins

The extra-Amazonian territory of Southern and South-Eastern Brazil constitutes a topographically diverse macro-region delimited to the east by the Atlantic Ocean, to the north by the São Francisco and Tocantins divides, and to the west by the Paraguay depression and the Argentine Pampas. The structural spine of the region is formed by the Atlantic Plateau, dominated by the crystalline scarps of the Serra do Mar and Serra da Mantiqueira, which rise abruptly from narrow coastal strips to altitudes between 800 and 2.800 metres above sea level. This mountainous barrier separates maritime drainage systems from the vast interior hydrographic networks of the La Plata basin.

West of the coastal escarpments, the landscape slopes gently toward the interior across the basaltic plateau of the Upper Paraná basin, drained by major tributaries including the Tietê, Paranapanema, Ivaí and Iguaçu rivers. Further north, the Paranaíba and Rio Grande merge to form the Paraná proper, cutting through extensive sandstone plateaux and fertile volcanic soils (*terra roxa*). To the north-west lies the Pantanal depression, an immense tectonic basin of seasonal wetlands fed by the Upper Paraguay river, while to the south, the rolling basaltic hills and sedimentary plains of the Rio Grande do Sul Pampa merge with the drainage of the Uruguay river and the lagoon systems of Lagoa dos Patos and Lagoa Mirim.

## Marine Upwelling, Estuaries and Coastal Lagoons

The southern and south-eastern Atlantic coastline exhibits profound hydrologic and marine variation. South of Cabo Frio, the South Atlantic Central Water upwelling creates rich marine feeding grounds that nourish vast shoals of small pelagic fishes, predatory sciaenids and marine mammals. Enclosed bays and estuarine complexes, including Guanabara Bay, the Baixada Santista, the Paranaguá estuary and the Santa Catarina lagoon systems (Laguna and Babitonga), provided stable, highly concentrated supplies of bivalves, crabs and fish.

This exceptional maritime biomass enabled early Holocene populations to establish enduring settlements without agricultural inputs. Stable isotope analyses and zooarchaeological excavations reveal that coastal shell-mound occupants derived upwards of 70 percent of their dietary protein from marine and estuarine resources [@lima2000em; @toso2021fishing]. The stability of these aquatic ecosystems dampened the seasonal vulnerability typical of terrestrial hunting, permitting long-term residential stability and multi-generational accumulation of monumental shell architecture [@bailey2002coastal; @deblasis2007some].

## Highland Araucária Forests and Cerrado Plateaux

Above the coastal scarps, between 600 and 1.400 metres altitude, the subtropical highlands experience temperate regimes with frequent winter frosts and high annual rainfall. During the mid to late Holocene, particularly after 1000BC, cooler and moister climatic conditions drove a dramatic expansion of the Brazilian pine forest (*Araucária angustifolia*) at the expense of highland grasslands (*campos*) [@iriarte2016emergent]. The large, energy-dense seeds (*pinhão*) of *Araucária angustifolia*, containing over 35 percent starch and rich in minerals, constituted a dependable carbohydrate staple available in profusion each autumn.

Further inland, the transition to the Central Cerrado across Goiás and western Minas Gerais features open savanna woodlands broken by gallery forests along perennial watercourses. These interior river valleys provided alluvial hunting and gathering corridors that later supported ring-village ceramic agriculturalists of the Aratu-Sapucaí tradition, who cultivated maize, manioc and tubers along floodplain terraces [@robrahn1996tradicao].

## Fluvial Systems of the Upper Paraná Basin and Southern Wetlands

The drainage architecture of the Upper Paraná basin exerted a defining influence on demographic distribution and inter-regional mobility. Flowing south-westward from the crystalline interior plateaux, the Tietê, Paranapanema and Iguaçu rivers carved wide alluvial valleys through basaltic lava flows, creating rich bottomland soils renewed by seasonal inundations. These riverine arteries functioned as primary trunk routes for canoe transit, connecting interior foraging territories with the sub-Andean foothill corridors and the Atlantic coast.

In the far south, the hydrographic complex of the Uruguay River and the coastal lagoon system formed an interconnected hydrologic landscape. The Uruguay River, punctuated by rapids and basaltic narrows, provided exceptional seasonal fisheries during spawning migrations (*piracema*), while the vast brackish expanses of Lagoa dos Patos (spanning over 10.000 km²) and Lagoa Mirim offered rich estuarine foraging zones. In the north-west, the Pantanal wetland covered over 140.000 km² of low-gradient floodplain, where annual flood pulses of two to four metres submerged up to 80 percent of the land surface between December and May, necessitating specialized elevated settlement forms.

These hydrological cycles imposed strict seasonal rhythms on regional labour allocation and resource procurement. During falling flood stages (*vazante*), receding waters trapped immense quantities of fish in oxbow lagoons and shallow channels, enabling intensive netting and poison-fishing expeditions that supplied villages with dried protein reserves. Conversely, during peak flood pulses (*enchente*), terrestrial game congregated on elevated natural levees and artificial mounds (*aterros* and *cerritos*), providing concentrated hunting targets that offset the temporary submergence of agricultural plots.

## Phytogeographic Zones: Atlantic Rainforest, Araucária Moist Forests and Cerrado

The botanical mosaic of Southern and South-Eastern Brazil comprised three primary floristic dominions that determined local carrying capacities and subsistence schedules. Along the Atlantic littoral and coastal mountains, the Dense Ombrophilous Forest (Mata Atlântica) supported high biodiversity, offering palms (*Euterpe edulis*), wild fruits (*Eugenia*, *Myrciaria*) and game, though canopy density restricted ground-level foraging. On the southern plateau, the Mixed Ombrophilous Forest formed dense stands of *Araucária angustifolia* intermixed with yerba mate (*Ilex paraguariensis*) and Lauraceae laurels, creating open understories favourable for deer and wild boar.

In the interior uplands of São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Goiás, the Semi-deciduous Seasonal Forest and Cerrado savanna formed a shifting ecotone. Gallery forests flanking river courses contained high concentrations of game and fertile alluvial soils suitable for swidden cultivation, while the surrounding savanna woodlands (*cerrado sensu stricto*) supplied seasonal fruits (*Caryocar brasiliense*, *Dipteryx alata*) and small game exploited during winter hunting excursions.

## Altitudinal Zonation and Micro-Climatic Refugia

Topographic relief created pronounced altitudinal stratification across Southern and South-Eastern Brazil, establishing distinct thermal and hydrological belts. The littoral lowlands below 100 metres altitude enjoyed maritime-buffered climates with year-round warmth, supporting perennial estuarine foraging and mangrove habitats. Ascending the Serra do Mar escarpment between 300 and 800 metres, persistent Atlantic cloud banks produced high atmospheric humidity and dense epiphyte growth, providing specialized plant resources such as bromeliad fibers, medicinal herbs and wild honey.

On the plateau above 900 metres, winter temperatures regularly dipped below freezing, with up to thirty frost nights annually during cold surges from Antarctic polar fronts. These montane conditions favoured the thermal strategy of semi-subterranean pit-houses (*casas subterrâneas*), which utilised the thermal inertia of subterranean clay soils to maintain interior temperatures several degrees above ambient winter chills [@schmitz2010casas]. Sheltered valley bottoms and north-facing slope facets provided micro-climatic refugia where maize crops were protected from early frosts, enabling double-cropping schedules in favourable seasons.

## Paleoclimatic Dynamics: Mid-Holocene Aridity and Late Holocene Pluvial

Palaeoenvironmental records derived from speleothems, lake cores and fossil pollen profiles illuminate significant climatic oscillations that altered prehistoric carrying capacities across Southern Brazil. Between 6000BC and 3000BC, a pronounced mid-Holocene dry phase reduced rainfall across the interior plateaux, causing contraction of gallery forests and seasonal drying of cerrado pans. This dry interval encouraged foraging populations to concentrate around perennial river channels and coastal estuaries, accelerating littoral demographic density and shell-mound aggregation.

Following 2000BC, intensification of the South American Monsoon System brought increased precipitation and cooler winters to southern latitudes [@iriarte2016emergent]. This late Holocene pluvial phase triggered the rapid downslope and northward expansion of *Araucária angustifolia* forests across Paraná, Santa Catarina and northern Rio Grande do Sul. The resulting expansion of pine nut biomass provided the ecological foundation for the demic growth of Taquara-Itararé pit-house populations during the first millennium AD.

## Lithic Raw Material Distributions and Mineral Landscapes

The distribution of lithic raw materials shaped regional technological organisation and exchange networks across Southern Brazil. In the basaltic plateaux of Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, abundant volcanic rocks provided tough fine-grained basalts and diabases ideal for heavy chopping tools, percussion flakes and polished ground-stone axes. Amygdaloidal basalt cavities and hydrothermal veins yielded chalcedony, agate and jasper, utilised extensively by Umbu and Humaitá knappers for projectile points, scrapers and drills [@loponte2015fishtail].

Along the Atlantic coast, the crystalline rocks of the Serra do Mar supplied granites, gneisses and amphibolites utilised in the production of polished ceremonial artefacts, particularly zoomorphic sculptures (*zoolitos*), pestles and axes found within monumental sambaquis [@prous1992arqueologia]. In the sandstone basins of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, silicified sandstones and quartz crystals supported flake-tool industries adapted to riverine and savanna foraging.

# Demographic Trajectory from the Terminal Pleistocene to the European Threshold

## Terminal Pleistocene and Early Archaic Colonisation (10000BC to 5000BC)

Human occupation of Southern Brazil originated during the terminal Pleistocene, as indicated by fluted and fishtail projectile point assemblages (Umbu tradition) recovered across Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and the Uruguay basin [@bueno2015first; @loponte2015fishtail]. These mobile hunting bands operated at extremely low demographic densities, exploiting megafaunal remnants and woodland game along open plateau corridors. At the 10000BC benchmark, we estimate an aggregate regional population of 15.040 persons, representing a sparse baseline density of 0,0078 persons/km².

During the early Holocene warming period (9000BC to 6000BC), hunter-gatherer bands gradually consolidated their seasonal ranges. Lithic assemblages diversified to incorporate bifacial projectile points, scrapers and boleadeiras suitable for hunting cervids, peccaries and rodents. As riverine valleys and lagoon margins were increasingly occupied, regional numbers expanded to 24.640 persons in 9000BC, 60.160 in 7000BC and 98.240 in 6000BC. By 5000BC, with post-glacial sea levels stabilising near modern elevations, coastal exploitation intensified, lifting the regional aggregate to 158.000 persons.

This transition from specialised megafaunal predation to broad-spectrum aquatic and woodland foraging was accompanied by shifts in group mobility patterns. Rock-shelter sequences throughout the Rio Claro basin in São Paulo and the Uruguay headwaters document recurrent seasonal re-occupation by small foraging bands numbering 15 to 30 individuals. Stratified hearth features, butchered cervid remains and grinding slabs indicate systematic processing of wild legumes, palm nuts (*Acrocomia aculeata*) and tubers, foreshadowing the plant-tending practices that later emerged alongside ceramic technologies.

## The Climax of Atlantic Shell-Mound Monumentality (5000BC to 1000BC)

Between 5000BC and 1000BC, the Atlantic littoral of Santa Catarina, Paraná, São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro became the locus of one of the most remarkable hunter-gatherer demographic phenomena in the Americas: the emergence of monumental shell mounds or *sambaquis* [@gaspar2008dating; @rick2023shell]. While historically interpreted as mere refuse heaps, geoarchaeological and micromorphological investigations have demonstrated that the largest sambaquis were deliberately constructed monumental public works, serving as funerary acropolises, territorial markers and ritual platforms [@deblasis2007some; @villagran2014microstratigraphic].

In focal areas such as the Santa Catarina southern lagoons (Tubarao and Laguna), mounds reached extraordinary dimensions. The Sambaqui de Garopaba do Sul attained a height of 30 metres and a base diameter exceeding 150 metres, containing several hundred thousand cubic metres of shell, sediment and fish bone. Mortuary complexes within single mounds contain hundreds of articulated human burials accompanied by zoomorphic stone sculptures (*zoolitos*), polished bone ornaments and ochre [@fish2013monumental; @souza2003study].

This monumental activity was underpinned by unprecedented demographic concentration. In the Southern Atlantic Sambaqui belt, population rose from 31.175 persons in 5000BC to 66.650 in 3000BC and 90.300 in 1000BC. Concurrently, in the Southeast Atlantic Coast, population reached 74.400 in 3000BC and 100.800 in 1000BC. Across the entire Southern Brazilian territory, aggregate population climbed to 332.000 in 3000BC and 465.600 in 1000BC. Toward the close of the first millennium BC, marine regression, lagoon siltation and changing coastal morphology altered estuarine productivity, precipitating the decline of the classical sambaqui system and shifting settlements toward riverine and barrier-island environments [@wagner2014origins].

## The Ceramic Transition, Southern Proto-Jê Pit-Houses and Ring-Mounds (1000BC to 1000AD)

The first millennium BC and the early centuries of the Common Era witnessed the widespread adoption of ceramics and the emergence of distinct upland and wetland socio-political organisations. In the subtropical highlands of Paraná, Santa Catarina and northern Rio Grande do Sul, groups belonging to the Taquara-Itararé tradition, ancestral to the Southern Jê (Kaingang and Xokleng), constructed nucleated villages comprising sunken semi-subterranean houses (*casas subterrâneas*) [@corteletti2015landscape; @schmitz2010casas].

These pit-houses, excavated from 1 to 7 metres in depth and up to 20 metres in diameter, were roofed with timber and thatch, providing thermal insulation against severe highland winters. At sites such as Abreu e Garcia and Pinhal da Serra, pit-houses are arranged in tight clusters adjacent to geometric earthworks, including circular dance grounds and paired funerary mounds enclosed by earthen rings (*estruturas anelares*) [@souza2016understanding; @souza2020genesis]. This architectural fluorescence coincided with intensive harvesting and management of *Araucária angustifolia* stands and the cultivation of maize and squash, supporting demographic expansion across the Tietê, Paranapanema and Iguaçu uplands, where population reached 136.800 in 0AD and 236.550 in 1000AD.

Simultaneously, in the lowlands surrounding Lagoa dos Patos and the Mirim basin, earthen mounds known as *cerritos* were constructed across wetland marshes [@milheira2017monumental; @milheira2019lowland]. Functioning as habitation platforms, cemetery loci and ceremonial centres, the cerritos supported dense communities exploiting marshland fish, rodents (capybara and coypu) and waterfowl, integrating local pottery traditions with seasonal foraging.

## The Guarani and Tupinambá Expansions (1000AD to 1500AD)

The final pre-contact half-millennium was defined by the rapid territorial expansion of Tupi-Guarani horticulturalists [@noelli1998tupi; @schmitz1991migrantes]. Originating from Southwestern Amazonia, Guarani populations moved southward along the Paraguay and Paraná river systems, colonising the alluvial floodplains of the Paranapanema, Tietê, Iguaçu and Uruguay basins, and ultimately breaching the coastal lowlands [@bonomo2015expansion]. Simultaneously, Tupinambá and Tupiniquim groups expanded along the Atlantic coastline from north to south, occupying fertile coastal plains and displacing or assimilating earlier resident groups.

The Tupi-Guarani economic package combined slash-and-burn polyculture of bitter and sweet manioc, maize, beans and sweet potatoes with intensive riverine and coastal fishing. Their settlements consisted of fortified villages composed of four to eight massive multi-family communal houses (*malocas*), surrounded by wooden palisades (*taipas*) and defensive ditches. Major contact-period settlements, such as Guanabara in Rio de Janeiro (5.154 peak inhabitants), São Vicente in Santos (3.073 peak inhabitants), and the Guaíra and Foz do Iguaçu clusters along the Paraná (exceeding 3.000 inhabitants each), represented formidable regional demographic centres.

Between 1000AD and 1500AD, aggregate population in Southern Brazil grew from 989.600 to 1.200.000 persons, with the Tietê-Paranapanema-Iguaçu corridor becoming the most populous sub-region (285.000 persons), followed by the Southeast Atlantic Coast (240.000 persons) and the Southern Atlantic Sambaqui belt (215.000 persons).

# Quantitative Gazetting and Sub-Regional Demographic Anchors

## The Six Pre-Columbian Sub-Regions

Operation Viscount partitions the 1.920.483 km² Southern Brazilian macro-region into six hydrologically and ecologically bounded units. Each sub-region reflects distinct environmental adaptations, archaeological facies and carrying capacity constraints:

1. *Southeast Atlantic Coast (Doce, Paraíba do Sul and Guanabara)*: Covering 259.847 km², this zone encompasses the narrow coastal lowlands and coastal cordilleras of Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo and eastern Minas Gerais. The 277 catalogued sites include coastal sambaquis, lagoon stations and extensive Tupinambá villages. Population expanded from 2.880 in 10000BC to 115.200 in 0AD and 240.000 in 1500AD (density 0,92 persons/km²).

2. *Southern Atlantic Sambaqui and Lagoa dos Patos Belt*: Spanning 231.713 km² from São Paulo through Paraná and Santa Catarina to the oceanic outlet of Lagoa dos Patos, this sub-region preserves the greatest density of monumental shell mounds in South America. The gazetteer catalogues 419 sites, including giant sambaquis (Garopaba do Sul, Jabuticabeira II, Cabeçuda) and late Tupiniquim settlements (São Vicente). Population reached 215.000 in 1500AD (density 0,93 persons/km²).

3. *Upper Paraná, Paranaíba and Central Cerrado*: Encompassing 357.528 km² across the highland savannas of Goiás, the Triângulo Mineiro and eastern Mato Grosso do Sul, this inland plateau supported 129 catalogued sites of the Aratu-Sapucaí ceramic tradition, characterised by circular village layouts. Population grew from 2.870 in 10000BC to 84.050 in 0AD and 205.000 in 1500AD (density 0,57 persons/km²).

4. *Tietê, Paranapanema and Iguaçu*: Covering 457.742 km² across São Paulo, Paraná and western Santa Catarina, this basin formed the primary demographic axis of the interior. The 415 catalogued sites document extensive Taquara-Itararé pit-house villages in the highlands and dense Guarani settlements along river terraces. Population reached 285.000 in 1500AD (density 0,62 persons/km²).

5. *Pantanal and Upper Paraguay Basin*: Spanning 445.775 km² of wetland floodplains and surrounding cerrado uplands in Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul, this sub-region supported 65 catalogued sites, prominently artificial earthen mounds (*aterros*) that provided flood refugia during annual inundation cycles. Population expanded from 1.610 in 10000BC to 47.150 in 0AD and 115.000 in 1500AD (density 0,26 persons/km²).

6. *Uruguay Basin and Rio Grande do Sul Pampa*: Encompassing 167.878 km² of rolling grasslands, deciduous riverine forest and southern basaltic plateaux, this border zone includes 177 catalogued sites representing Umbu lithic camps, Taquara-Itararé highland earthworks and late prehistoric Guarani settlements. Population reached 140.000 in 1500AD (density 0,83 persons/km²).

## Urban Aggregations and Nucleation Thresholds

Unlike the dense pre-contact agrarian states of the Central Andes, nucleated settlements in Southern Brazil were constrained by soil nutrient depletion under tropical swidden regimes and the carrying capacity of estuarine shellfish beds. Nonetheless, archaeological mapping and ethnohistorical sources confirm that regional populations achieved substantial local aggregations:

- *Guanabara (Karióka Tupinambá)*: A network of interconnected fortified villages located around Guanabara Bay, with an aggregate contact population estimated at 2.613 persons in 1500AD and a cumulative peak footprint supporting over 5.100 individuals across its constituent malocas.
- *Guaíra (Guairá Guarani)*: Situated along the rich alluvial terraces of the Upper Paraná River above the Sete Quedas cascades, this settlement complex supported 1.909 inhabitants in 1500AD (peak 3.796), sustained by productive riverine fisheries and intensive maize-manioc horticulture.
- *Foz do Iguaçu (Guarani Paraná)*: Positioned at the confluence of the Iguaçu and Paraná rivers, controlling vital canoe navigation routes and fertile alluvial soils, with a contact population of 1.708 persons (peak 3.392).
- *São Vicente (Guaibê Tupiniquim)*: A maritime horticultural hub on the Santos estuarine island, supporting 1.558 persons in 1500AD (peak 3.073).
- *São Miguel (Uruguai Guarani)*: A nucleated riverine centre along the Middle Uruguay basin, supporting 1.306 persons in 1500AD (peak 2.557).
- *Pinhal da Serra (Southern Jê)*: A highland civic-ceremonial cluster comprising dozens of semi-subterranean pit-houses and enclosing earthworks, supporting 955 inhabitants in 1500AD (peak 1.876).
- *Goiânia (Aratu-Sapucaí)*: An inland ring-village complex featuring circular house arrangements around a central plaza, supporting 904 persons in 1500AD (peak 1.761).

# Archaeological Horizons, Material Culture and Subsistence Economies

## Sambaqui Coastal Architecture and Mortuary Ritual

The monumental shell mounds of the southern coast represent complex socio-ecological constructions that evolved over four millennia. Stratigraphic excavations at Jabuticabeira II, Cabeçuda and Santa Marta have demonstrated that mound accumulation resulted from deliberate, phased deposition of marine shell (*Anomalocardia brasiliana*, *Crassostrea rhizophorae*), fish bones and sediment [@klokler2010juntos; @mendes2026food]. These deposits were intercalated with formal burning horizons and structured burial features containing multiple secondary and primary interments.

Zooarchaeological records confirm that teleost fishes, particularly whitemouth croaker (*Micropogonias furnieri*) and sea catfish (*Ariidae*), constituted the primary dietary staple, supplemented by sharks, rays, marine mammals and seasonal molluscs [@toso2021fishing]. Whaling activities, primarily involving stranded or coastal-migrating southern right whales (*Eubalaena australis*), contributed substantial lipid and blubber resources, with whale bones frequently repurposed as grave markers and architectural retaining elements [@lopes2016the].

Palaeopathological analyses of sambaqui skeletal series reveal low frequencies of dental caries (below 3 percent), reflecting diets low in fermentable carbohydrates, but moderate to high frequencies of auditory exostoses (swimmer's ear), indicative of continuous cold-water diving [@souza2003study]. Osteological markers of physical stress document heavy biomechanical loads associated with paddling and water transport. Genetic and craniometric studies confirm morphological continuity among sambaqui populations over millennia, until late-Holocene interactions introduced ceramic-producing populations from the interior [@marinho2006paleogenet].

## Paleoparasitology, Skeletal Pathology and Health Profiles

Coprolite investigations and paleoparasitological studies from coastal and rock-shelter sites provide direct bioarchaeological evidence of health conditions and endemic disease loads in Pre-Columbian Southern Brazil [@ferreira2014foundations]. The recovery of helminth eggs, including *Ancylostoma duodenale*, *Trichuris trichiura* and *Enterobius vermicularis*, from desiccated coprolites confirms that intestinal parasitism was established in regional populations well before European trans-oceanic contact. High population concentrations on monumental sambaquis, coupled with damp shell-matrix environments, facilitated the transmission of soil-transmitted helminths.

Skeletal pathology across southern series indicates marked differences in epidemiological stress between littoral foragers and interior agriculturalists. Sambaqui series exhibit high rates of degenerative osteoarthritis in the lumbar spine, shoulders and knees, reflecting strenuous physical labour in open-water navigation and shell procurement. Traumatic lesions, including healed cranial fractures and parry fractures of the ulna, appear in 5 to 12 percent of adult males, indicating interpersonal violence. In contrast, late prehistoric agricultural series (Guarani and Aratu) display sharp increases in cribra orbitalia and porotic hyperostosis (reaching 25 to 35 percent), indicating childhood nutritional stress, anaemia and parasitic infection associated with sedentary village life and weaning diets dominated by maize porridge.

## Shell-Midden Zooarchaeology and Malacological Diversity

Malacological assemblages from the Atlantic littoral provide detailed records of Holocene shoreline ecology, sea-surface temperatures and human exploitation strategies [@rick2023shell; @wagner2014origins]. Excavations in Santa Catarina and Paraná reveal that early sambaqui horizons (5000BC to 3000BC) were dominated by estuarine bivalves, principally *Anomalocardia brasiliana* (upwards of 80 percent of shell volume) and mangrove oysters (*Crassostrea rhizophorae*), accompanied by the mud snail *Heleobia australis* and edible clams (*Lucina pectinata*, *Tivela mactroides*).

In late archaic and formative horizons (2000BC to 500BC), changing coastal geomorphology and marine regression altered local shell collection patterns [@mendes2026food]. Open-coast rocky-shore species, such as brown mussels (*Perna perna*) and limpets (*Fissurella*), increased in frequency, alongside larger marine gastropods (*Adelomelon brasiliana*, *Olivancillaria*) utilised both for meat and for fashioning beads, perforators and fishing weights. Terrestrial gastropods, including giant land snails (*Thaumastus*), occur in mortuary strata, reflecting deliberate deposition during funerary feasting rather than adventitious intrusions [@simone2025already].

## Lithic Technologies and Ground Stone Industries

Lithic production systems in Southern Brazil display clear economic adaptations to regional ecosystems [@bueno2015first; @loponte2015fishtail]. Early Holocene Umbu assemblages across the southern grasslands and river valleys featured small bifacial projectile points with expanding stems, retouched scrapers and microliths made from chalcedony and silicified wood. These toolkits were supplemented by polished spherical stones utilised as hunting projectiles in boleadeiras (*boleadeiras de duas ou três pedras*), designed for capturing rhea and pampa deer.

In the interior forests and coastal escarpments, Humaitá tradition assemblages were dominated by large, unifacially flaked basalt and diabase core tools (*talhadores* and *raspadores*) adapted to heavy wood-working, tree-felling and dugout canoe manufacturing. With the emergence of sedentism and horticulture during the late Holocene, ground and polished stone tools proliferated. Symmetrical petaloid and rectangular stone celts, fashioned from tough metabasalt and diorite, became standard implements for clearing swidden plots and constructing timber-framed communal longhouses [@prous1992arqueologia].

Lithic procurement required dedicated expeditions to primary quarry outcrops in the crystalline escarpments and river gravel deposits. High-grade chalcedonies and agates from the Botucatu and Serra Geral formations were transported over distances exceeding 150 kilometres, moving across sub-regional boundaries through reciprocal gift exchange. In coastal sambaquis, the presence of polished nephrite and jadeite lip-plugs (*tembetás*) demonstrates long-distance prestige-goods networks connecting littoral populations with interior metamorphic sources.

## Aquatic Adaptations: Canoe Navigation and Fishing Gear

The maintenance of high demographic densities across both the coastal lagoon systems and the interior river basins depended upon advanced aquatic transport and fishing technology [@astrup2019underwater; @bailey2008archaeology]. Indigenous groups constructed large monoxylous dugout canoes (*ubás* and *canoas*) carved from trunks of native cedrela (*Cedrela fissilis*), yellow poui (*Handroanthus serratifolius*) and ocotea. Capable of transporting 15 to 40 individuals along coastal bays or across turbulent river rapids, these watercraft enabled regular trade and coordinated military expeditions.

Fishing gear recovered from dry cave contexts, waterlogged wetland sites and shell matrix includes bi-pointed bone gorges (*anzóis retos*), composite bone and shell fishhooks, woven vegetal fiber nets and carved bone harpoon points [@mendes2026food]. In estuarine shallows and river meanders, communities constructed extensive wooden and brushwood weirs (*pari*) that trapped migrating fish schools on falling tides or seasonal river recession, providing massive food surpluses preserved through smoke-curing on elevated wooden barbecues (*moquéns*).

## Ceramic Typologies: Taquara, Itararé, Una and Tupiguarani Horizons

The ceramic sequence of Southern and South-Eastern Brazil comprises four primary technological traditions reflecting distinct linguistic and cultural traditions:

1. *Taquara-Itararé Tradition*: Associated with Southern Proto-Jê populations in the southern plateau and coastal highlands. Vessels are small to medium-sized (5 to 30 litres capacity), thin-walled (3 to 6 mm), tempered with fine sand or crushed quartz, and fired in reducing atmospheres. Decorative treatments include punctate stamping, fingertip impressions, incision and red slips, closely associated with domestic pit-house assemblages and mortuary enclosures [@schmitz2010casas; @souza2020genesis].

2. *Una Tradition*: Distributed across the coastal cordilleras of Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo and eastern Minas Gerais, primarily in rock-shelters and small open-air sites. Una ceramics are thin, dark, hemispherical bowls and small cooking pots tempered with crushed mica or sand, associated with mobile forest foragers who maintained broad-spectrum hunting and gathering while adopting limited horticulture [@prous1992arqueologia].

3. *Aratu-Sapucaí Tradition*: Prominent across the Central Cerrado of Goiás, the Triângulo Mineiro and north-western São Paulo. Aratu ceramics comprise large, thick-walled, piriform and globular vessels (exceeding 80 litres capacity) with conical or flat bases, plain smoothed surfaces and thickened rims, adapted to large-scale maize storage, beer fermentation and mortuary urn burial within circular plaza settlements [@robrahn1996tradicao].

4. *Tupiguarani Tradition*: Extensive along the major fluvial axes of the Paraná, Uruguay and Paraíba do Sul basins and the Atlantic littoral. Characterised by composite-silhouette carinated bowls, large funerary urns (*igaçabas*) and massive beer-brewing vats (*yapepó*), adorned with polychrome red, black and white painted motifs, corrugation, brushing and ungulate fingernail impressions [@bonomo2015expansion; @noelli1998tupi].

## Taquara-Itararé Highland Architecture and Forest Management

In the Araucária plateau, the Taquara-Itararé tradition represents a specialised highland adaptation that coordinated domestic habitation, funerary monumentalism and silviculture [@iriarte2016emergent; @souza2016understanding]. Pit-houses were excavated into hillsides and plateau crests, often organised in circular or linear clusters that accommodated extended kinship units. At the site of Abreu e Garcia in Santa Catarina, paired subterranean structures exceeded 10 metres in diameter, containing multiple central hearths, ceramic roasting vessels and charred *Araucária angustifolia* seeds [@corteletti2015landscape].

Monumental earthworks associated with the Taquara-Itararé tradition comprise circular earthen enclosures (*estruturas anelares*) ranging from 20 to 120 metres in diameter, often featuring sunken central avenues oriented toward prominent topographic features [@souza2020genesis]. Excavations within these enclosures demonstrate their primary funerary and ceremonial function: low central mounds enclose cremated human remains placed within ceramic urns, associated with feasting debris that includes thousands of carbonised pine seeds and mammal bones. Radiocarbon chronologies establish that earthwork construction intensified dramatically after 1000AD, reflecting heightened social competition, territorial demarcation and population growth within the highland pine forests.

## Tupiguarani Fluvial Polyculture and Territoriality

The arrival of Guarani and Tupinambá populations transformed the demographic geography of Southern Brazil through the introduction of intensive swidden horticulture and expansive multi-village alliances [@noelli1998tupi; @schmitz1991migrantes]. Tupiguarani ceramics, characterised by polychrome red-and-black painting on white slip, large globular cooking vessels and enormous fermentation vats (*yapepó*), reflect social systems organised around communal labour, reciprocal feasting and regional ritual exchange.

Settlement surveys in the Paraná and Paranapanema basins reveal dense linear settlement arrays situated on well-drained river terraces above seasonal flood lines [@bonomo2015expansion]. Individual villages featured large communal longhouses (*malocas*) measuring up to 60 metres in length and 15 metres in width, constructed of heavy timber frameworks roofed with palm thatch. The internal space of each maloca was partitioned among nuclear family hearths, accommodating 50 to 150 related individuals. Fortified settlements incorporated perimeter palisades, external pit traps and earthen embankments, documenting persistent endemic warfare between competing regional confederacies.

The Guarani agricultural calendar integrated bitter manioc cultivation along secondary terraces with alluvial maize planting timed to exploit seasonal river recession. Forest foraging, particularly hunting of tapir, peccary and howler monkey, was combined with intensive riverine fish-trapping and netting, supporting regional population densities between 1 and 2,5 persons/km² along major river corridors.

## Cerritos and Wetland Raised Architecture

In the subtropical wetlands of Rio Grande do Sul and the Pantanal, indigenous populations engineered earthen platforms to mitigate severe seasonal inundation. The *cerritos* of the Mirim and Patos lagoons comprise circular and elliptical earthen mounds ranging from 1 to 5 metres in elevation and 20 to 80 metres in length, constructed from local clay, organic refuse and freshwater mussel shells [@milheira2017monumental; @milheira2019lowland].

Micromorphological analyses show that cerritos functioned as long-term residential bases where domestic structures were raised above surrounding marshes. These mounds also served as community cemeteries, accumulating tens of primary and secondary burials over centuries. Subsistence was centred on the exploitation of wetland resources, including giant otter, capybara, waterfowl and marsh fishes (*Hoplias malabaricus*), supplemented by wild plant gathering and small-scale cultivation of gourds and maize on elevated ground.

Similarly, in the Pantanal of Mato Grosso do Sul, pre-contact communities constructed artificial earthen mounds (*aterros*) along the banks of the Paraguay, Cuiabá and Miranda rivers [@eremites2002prehistoria; @peixoto2003populacoes]. These elevated habitation stations, belonging to ceramic traditions such as Pantanal and Descalvados, provided year-round refugia during the six-month flood season, supporting sedentary communities that engaged in intensive aquatic foraging, turtle hunting and seasonal hunting of flooded-out savanna fauna.

# Methodological Integration and Palaeodemographic Uncertainty

## Radiocarbon Chronologies and Reservoir Offsets

The reconstruction of demographic trends in Southern Brazil relies upon a composite radiocarbon framework comprising over 1.200 published 14C determinations calibrated using the SHCal20 atmospheric curve and the Marine20 marine calibration curve. In marine and estuarine contexts, the interpretation of radiocarbon dates from sambaquis requires rigorous correction for local marine reservoir effects ($\Delta R$).

Studies of pre-bomb marine shells along the south-eastern and southern coasts indicate substantial spatial variation in $\Delta R$ values, driven by coastal upwelling dynamics and estuarine freshwater dilution [@gaspar2008dating; @villagran2014microstratigraphic]. In upwelling zones such as Cabo Frio and southern Santa Catarina, $\Delta R$ offsets range from -150 to +250 years, necessitating paired charcoal-shell dating to establish secure chronological sequences. In highland contexts, radiocarbon dates derived from *Araucária angustifolia* charcoal are subject to old-wood effects, given the multi-century lifespans of mature pine trees, requiring careful selection of short-lived botanical remains (such as carbonised seeds and twig wood) for stratigraphic dating [@iriarte2016emergent; @souza2016understanding].

## Taphonomic Constraints and Archaeological Visibility

Archaeological visibility in Southern Brazil is shaped by severe taphonomic and geomorphological asymmetries:

1. *Mid-Holocene Marine Transgression*: The Santos Transgression (reaching approximately +2,5 metres above modern sea level around 3500BC) submerged early Holocene coastal sites and reworked older barrier-lagoon formations [@bailey2008archaeology; @wagner2014origins]. Consequently, pre-6000BC coastal settlements are under-represented, with early coastal exploitation largely inferred from inland shell middens and elevated barrier deposits.

2. *High-Energy Alluvial Reworking*: Riverine floodplains throughout the Upper Paraná, Tietê and Uruguay basins experience high annual discharge and dynamic sediment transport, which bury open-air Guarani campsites beneath metres of alluvium or erode river-terrace malocas.

3. *Highland Forest Cover and Soil Acidity*: In the Araucária plateau, dense subtropical forest canopy and highly acidic latosols (pH 4 to 5,2) accelerate the decomposition of unburned organic matter and non-mineralised skeletal remains. While stone tool industries and earthen earthworks remain visible, bone tool assemblages and non-charred botanical remains are rarely preserved outside calcareous shell matrices or saturated wetland deposits.

4. *Asymmetric Survey Intensity*: Modern infrastructural development and academic research intensity create spatial unevenness in site registration. The coastal sambaqui zones of Santa Catarina and the metropolitan hinterlands of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro have received over a century of intensive archaeological survey, yielding hundreds of documented sites. Conversely, the vast forested tracts of the interior Paraná basin and the remote floodplains of the Pantanal remain comparatively under-sampled, requiring model-based spatial smoothing to compensate for uneven survey coverage.

## Carrying Capacity Modelling and Spatial Kriging

To reconcile discrete site gazetteers with continuous regional population surfaces, Operation Viscount implements a non-stationary Matérn kriging framework conditioned on hydrological sub-basins, elevation models and ethnohistorical carrying capacity envelopes. In littoral zones, carrying capacity was parameterized as a linear function of shoreline length and estuarine surface area, with maximum sustainable densities capped at 3,5 persons per linear kilometre of productive coast. In the Araucária highlands, carrying capacity was scaled to pine stand density and mast-year frequencies, with baseline densities capped at 1,2 persons/km².

In the interior alluvial corridors of the Paraná, Paranapanema and Uruguay rivers, carrying capacity models incorporated soil fertility parameters (*terra roxa* distribution) and flood recession agricultural potential, permitting local cluster densities up to 2,5 persons/km² while maintaining regional watershed densities between 0,55 and 0,85 persons/km². This stratified spatial approach prevents artificial over-smoothing across major ecological divides, such as the precipitous transition between the Atlantic coastal plain and the high Serra do Mar.

## Settlement Size-Frequency Distributions and Zipfian Scaling

Analysis of settlement size-frequency distributions across the 1.482 catalogued pre-contact sites in Southern Brazil illuminates macro-regional political organisation and demographic centralization. When ranked by estimated contact population, the gazetteer exhibits a log-normal distribution characterized by a moderately steep rank-size slope ($\alpha \approx 0,88$). This distribution departs from strict Zipfian primacy, reflecting the absence of a single overarching regional metropolis.

Instead, the settlement hierarchy features two prominent primary nodes: Guanabara along the Atlantic littoral (supporting 2.613 persons at contact with a cumulative multi-village footprint of 5.154 persons) and Guaíra along the Upper Paraná (supporting 1.909 persons at contact and 3.796 at peak). Beneath these leading centres, an extensive intermediate tier of regional hubs (including Foz do Iguaçu, São Vicente, São Miguel, Porto Seguro, Piratininga and Pinhal da Serra, each housing between 900 and 1.800 persons) coordinated local exchange networks. This polycentric pattern reflects multi-focal chiefdoms and tribal confederacies adapted to distinct ecological niches, where political authority was confederated rather than bureaucratic.

## Ethnohistorical Contact Baselines and Depopulation Trajectories

The 1500AD demographic benchmark of 1.200.000 persons is corroborated by early European contact chronicles and subsequent colonial documentation from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries [@noelli1999ocupacao]. Early Portuguese navigation logs along the coast, including Pero Vaz de Caminha's 1500 letter and the 1530-1532 accounts of Martim Afonso de Sousa at São Vicente, record continuous coastal settlement by Tupiniquim and Tupinambá groups with individual villages comprising hundreds of inhabitants. In Rio de Janeiro, French narratives from the Villegaignon expedition (Jean de Léry and André Thevet) describe Guanabara Bay as inhabited by dozens of allied Tupinambá villages capable of mobilising thousands of warriors.

In the interior, Spanish expeditions under Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca (1541-1542) traversing Santa Catarina and Paraná toward Asunción documented densely populated Guarani provinces along the Iguaçu and Tibagi rivers, reporting continuous cultivated fields of maize and manioc. Subsequent Jesuit mission censuses in the Guairá province during the early seventeenth century recorded over 100.000 baptized Guarani across thirteen reducciones before their destruction by São Paulo bandeirante slave raids. Incorporating devastating virgin-soil epidemics (smallpox, measles and influenza) that swept through southern Brazil from 1554 onward, ethnohistorical depopulation ratios between 80 and 95 percent indicate a pre-contact regional population comfortably in the range of 1M to 1,4M persons, fully consistent with our baseline estimate of 1.200.000 inhabitants.

# Sources
